summary.text: Take the counterexample \(n=736>599\). If its largest attainable least base exceeded \(7\), then \(736\) would be a sum of at most four squares whose nonzero bases all lie in \(\{8,\ldots,27\}\); padding with zeros reduces this to a finite search over \(\{0,8,\ldots,27\}^4\), which finds no such quadruple, so \(a(736)\le 7\).

full_proof.text:
Let us spell out the definition relevant to the conjecture. For a positive integer \(k\), call \(k\) admissible for \(n\) if there is a nonempty nondecreasing list
\[
 b_1\le b_2\le\cdots\le b_r,\qquad 1\le r\le 4,
\]
of nonnegative integers such that
\[
 b_1^2+b_2^2+\cdots+b_r^2=n
\]
and \(b_1=k\). Then \(a(n)\) is the largest admissible \(k\) (with value \(0\) if there is no admissible \(k\)). Thus, if \(a(n)>7\), the maximum itself is an admissible integer \(m>7\), and there is a representation of \(n\) by at most four nondecreasing squares all of whose bases are at least \(m\), hence greater than \(7\).

We disprove the conjecture using
\[
 n=736.
\]
Certainly \(736>599\). We will prove that \(a(736)\le 7\).

The key fact is the following finite obstruction.

**Claim.** There do not exist four integers
\[
 x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\in B:=\{0,8,9,\ldots,27\}
\]
such that
\[
 x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2+x_4^2=736. \tag{1}
\]

We prove the claim without assuming that the \(x_i\) are ordered.

First note that \(736\) is divisible by \(16\). A square modulo \(16\) is one of \(0,1,4,9\). In fact, all four \(x_i\) in (1) must be even. To see this, it is enough first to work modulo \(8\). An odd square is \(1\pmod 8\), while an even square is \(0\) or \(4\pmod 8\). If exactly one or exactly three of the \(x_i\) were odd, the sum of their squares would be odd, contrary to (1). If exactly two were odd, their two squares would contribute \(2\pmod 4\), while the two even squares would contribute \(0\pmod 4\), again impossible because \(736\equiv0\pmod4\). If all four were odd, their squares would sum to \(4\pmod8\), whereas \(736\equiv0\pmod8\). Hence none is odd.

For an even integer \(x\), its square is \(0\pmod{16}\) when \(4\mid x\), and is \(4\pmod{16}\) when \(x\equiv2\pmod4\). If exactly \(t\) of the four numbers are congruent to \(2\pmod4\), the sum of the four squares is \(4t\pmod{16}\). Since \(0\le t\le4\) and the sum is \(0\pmod{16}\), one must have either \(t=0\) or \(t=4\). Consequently there are only two cases:

1. all four \(x_i\) are divisible by \(4\); or
2. all four \(x_i\) are congruent to \(2\pmod4\).

We eliminate these cases separately.

### Case 1: all four bases are divisible by \(4\)

The elements of \(B\) divisible by \(4\) are
\[
 0,8,12,16,20,24.
\]
Write \(x_i=4u_i\). Then
\[
 u_i\in\{0,2,3,4,5,6\},
\]
and dividing (1) by \(16\) gives
\[
 u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2+u_4^2=46. \tag{2}
\]
We show directly that (2) is impossible.

If some \(u_i=6\), there can be only one such term, and the other three squares must sum to
\[
 46-6^2=10.
\]
Each of those other squares must then be one of \(0,4,9\), because \(4^2,5^2,6^2>10\). If one of the three squares is \(9\), the remaining two would have to sum to \(1\), impossible using \(0,4,9\). If no square is \(9\), their sum is divisible by \(4\), so it cannot equal \(10\). Thus no \(u_i\) is \(6\).

Suppose next that some \(u_i=5\). Again there can be only one, since \(2\cdot25>46\), and the remaining three squares must sum to
\[
 46-5^2=21.
\]
The remaining entries lie in \(\{0,2,3,4\}\), with square values \(0,4,9,16\). Modulo \(4\), only the value \(9\) contributes \(1\). Since \(21\equiv1\pmod4\), exactly one of the three squares must be \(9\). (There cannot be five such terms, and among three terms the only nonnegative count congruent to \(1\pmod4\) is one.) The other two squares would then have to sum to \(12\), but two members of \(\{0,4,16\}\) can only have sums
\[
 0,4,8,16,20,32,
\]
not \(12\). Thus no \(u_i\) is \(5\).

It remains that every \(u_i\) belongs to \(\{0,2,3,4\}\), so every square is in \(\{0,4,9,16\}\). Reducing (2) modulo \(4\), the number of occurrences of \(9\) must be congruent to \(46\equiv2\pmod4\). Among four terms this means that exactly two squares are \(9\). Those two contribute \(18\), leaving
\[
 46-18=28
\]
for the other two squares. But the other two are selected from \(\{0,4,16\}\), whose possible two-term sums are again
\[
 0,4,8,16,20,32,
\]
and none is \(28\). This finishes Case 1.

### Case 2: all four bases are \(2\pmod4\)

The members of \(B\) congruent to \(2\pmod4\) are
\[
 10,14,18,22,26.
\]
Write \(x_i=2v_i\). Then
\[
 v_i\in\{5,7,9,11,13\},
\]
and dividing (1) by \(4\) yields
\[
 v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2+v_4^2=184. \tag{3}
\]
No \(v_i\) can equal \(13\), because then the left side would be at least
\[
 13^2+3\cdot5^2=169+75=244>184.
\]
Likewise no \(v_i\) can equal \(11\), because then it would be at least
\[
 11^2+3\cdot5^2=121+75=196>184.
\]
Therefore every \(v_i\) lies in \(\{5,7,9\}\).

Let \(a,b,c\) be the respective numbers of occurrences of \(5,7,9\). Then
\[
 a+b+c=4
\]
and (3) says
\[
 25a+49b+81c=184.
\]
Subtracting \(25(a+b+c)=100\) gives
\[
 24b+56c=84.
\]
The left side is divisible by \(8\), whereas \(84\) is not divisible by \(8\). This is impossible, completing Case 2 and proving the claim.

We now apply the claim to the sequence. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(a(736)>7\). By the definition of the maximum, there is an admissible value \(m=a(736)>7\) and a nondecreasing representation
\[
 b_1^2+\cdots+b_r^2=736,
 \qquad 1\le r\le4,
 \qquad b_1=m.
\]
Because the list is nondecreasing,
\[
 b_j\ge b_1=m>7
\]
for every \(j\). On the other hand, each square is one nonnegative summand of a sum equal to \(736\), so
\[
 b_j^2\le736.
\]
Since \(28^2=784>736\), this gives \(b_j\le27\). Thus every actual base \(b_j\) lies in \(\{8,9,\ldots,27\}\).

If \(r<4\), append \(4-r\) zero bases. We thereby obtain four elements of
\[
 B=\{0,8,9,\ldots,27\}
\]
whose squares still sum to \(736\). This contradicts the claim. Therefore
\[
 a(736)\le7.
\]

For completeness, the candidate set in the definition is not empty here: there is the nondecreasing representation
\[
 736=4^2+8^2+16^2+20^2
      =16+64+256+400,
\]
whose least base is \(4\). Hence \(a(736)\) is at least \(4\), although its exact value is unnecessary.

We have exhibited \(736>599\) for which \(a(736)\) is not greater than \(7\). Thus the statement
\[
 \forall n>599,\quad a(n)>7
\]
is false.
